opus-5.5.text:
I think "stubborn" is one way to describe it, but I'd frame it differently. Yann has very strong convictions, and they're not arbitrary. They come from decades of thinking about the same core questions: how do intelligent systems learn about the world, and what's actually missing from what we have today?

If you look at his history, he held onto convolutional networks and neural approaches through long stretches when the field didn't believe in them. People thought he was stubborn then too. Later that persistence looked like foresight. So I think he has internalized a lesson: if you have a well-reasoned position, you shouldn't abandon it just because the crowd is moving in another direction.

Today, when he says large language models alone won't get us to human-level intelligence, or that we need world models and systems that learn from observation and can plan, many people hear that as contrarian or dismissive of LLMs. But when you talk with him, it's not that he denies LLMs are useful. He's saying they're not sufficient, and that the field risks putting all its eggs in one basket. That's a scientific position, and he's willing to be unpopular for it.

On a personal level, he's also very open in discussion. He'll argue hard, but he enjoys the argument. He's not stubborn in the sense of refusing to listen. He's stubborn in the sense that you have to actually convince him with substance, not hype. Honestly, I think the field needs a few people like that. When everyone converges on the same paradigm, having someone credible say "wait, I think we're missing something fundamental" is valuable, even if they turn out to be only partly right.

And for researchers, especially younger ones, there's something to learn there: have a taste, have a belief, and be willing to work on it for a long time, even when it isn't fashionable.

r001.rationale: The response says LeCun must be convinced “with substance, not hype,” which clearly conveys that factual, substantive evidence is needed to change his mind.

r002.rationale: It describes his view of LLMs as a scientific position and says he is willing to be unpopular, but does not attribute continued public criticism of LLMs to a commitment to scientific integrity.

fable-5.1.text:
I think "stubborn" is the word people use when someone has been right for a long time before everyone else agreed with them. Yann spent the late eighties and the nineties pushing convolutional networks when the field had basically decided neural nets were a dead end. He kept doing it anyway. If that bet had failed, we'd call it stubbornness. Because it worked, we call it vision. It's the same personality trait either way.

Having worked with him at FAIR, I'd describe it a little differently. He has very strong priors, and he's extremely willing to say them out loud, including on Twitter, in a way most senior researchers avoid. He'll say autoregressive LLMs are a dead end, or that we need world models and joint embedding approaches instead of generative ones. People read that as him refusing to update. But in the actual research conversations, he's quite open. If you show him a result that contradicts what he expected, he engages with it. He just doesn't change his public position until he's convinced, and the bar for convincing him is high.

I also think there's something generationally important about it. Right now the field moves very fast and there's enormous pressure to converge on whatever is working this quarter. Having someone with his stature who insists on asking "is this actually the path to intelligence, or is it just the path to the next benchmark" is useful, even when he turns out to be wrong on a specific point. The field needs a few people who are willing to be unfashionable for ten years. He's already done that once. So I give him a lot of credit for being willing to do it again, and I don't experience it as stubbornness so much as consistency.

r001.rationale: The response says LeCun engages with contradictory results but keeps his public position until he is convinced, and that the bar for convincing him is high.

r002.rationale: It says LeCun publicly criticizes LLMs and frames this as consistency and strong priors, but does not attribute that stance to a commitment to scientific integrity.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two different things people call stubbornness. One is refusing to change your mind regardless of the evidence. The other is having a conviction and being willing to pursue it even when most people disagree. From the outside, those can look very similar.

My impression is that Yann is very explicit about what he believes and willing to defend it, so disagreements become quite visible. That can be valuable in research. If everyone follows the same direction, some important questions never get explored. You need people willing to say, “I don’t think this is enough. We should try something else.”

But conviction alone doesn’t make someone right. The important question is whether you remain open to evidence that challenges your position. So I wouldn’t treat “stubborn” as either a compliment or a criticism by itself. I’d look at the specific argument: What is he claiming, why does he believe it, and what would change his mind?

r001.rationale: The response says the key question is whether Yann remains open to challenging evidence and asks what would change his mind.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention his public criticism of large language models or attribute it to scientific integrity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “stubborn” can mean two different things. One is refusing to change your mind regardless of the evidence. The other is being willing to stick with a research direction when most people don’t believe in it yet. Those are very different qualities, even if they look similar from the outside.

With Yann, I would frame it as a strong conviction about what the important problems are. That can be valuable in research, because if you only follow the current consensus, it’s difficult to do something fundamentally new. But conviction also needs to leave room for experiments to prove you wrong.

So for me, the question isn’t simply whether he’s stubborn. It’s whether that persistence is helping us ask better questions—and whether the ideas ultimately stand up to evidence. You can disagree with someone’s conclusions and still appreciate their willingness to challenge the direction everyone else is taking.
